utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness can be brought in. We'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber has just finished hearing the evidence of a witness in closed session. We are now again in public session. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The next witness is Mr. Goran Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask, noting the time, whether it would be more practical to have the break now and then an hour and a quarter straight session, or would you like to start the witness now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would prefer to have the break now. That way we don't have to interrupt in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think then we'll have the second break now and resume at 5.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that's shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where and when were you born, Mr. Stoparic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I was born in Sremska Mitrovica in 1968, on the 17th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't getting interpretation, but now -- there. Mr. Stoparic, on 6th July, 2006, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you have the chance to review your statement before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And while reviewing your statement, did you make a number of corrections to your statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, in order to proceed efficiently through the corrections you've made to your statement, I'm going to read out the passages and ask you each time whether you agree with the corrected version of the text. The first correction, paragraph 4, second sentence currently reads: "In order to become a Vojvoda, you had to have 500 volunteers under your control." Did you correct the sentence to read: "In order to become a Vojvoda you had to have up to 500 volunteers under your control"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first version, it turned out that this was a limit. It was never like that. I added that it could be up to 500.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Second correction, paragraph 17, lines 2 and 3, currently read: "I reported to Mayor Boca. Boca reported to Legija, Mrgud, Frenki, and ultimately Stanisic." Did you correct this passage to read: "I reported to Mayor Boca, Boca reported to Mrgud, Legija reported to Frenki, and ultimately Stanisic"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I corrected it by saying that if I'm carrying out an assignment, I report to Mayor Boca or to Slobodan Medic who was the commander; and then he reported to Mrgud or Milan Milanovic who was then, I think, deputy minister of defence, and then Milan Milanovic further on. So I was never with Milan Milanovic when he was reporting to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll move to the next correction. Paragraph 27, lines 11 and 12 currently read: "I signed a six-month contract and then after a few months I signed a three-year contract with the Red Berets and JSO." Did you correct these lines to read: "If I had stayed with the Red Berets JSO for six months I would have signed a three-year contract, but I did not serve with the JSO for six months and did not sign a three-year contract"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I corrected it. I was, for a period, at Mount Tara for training, which was conducted by members of the Red Berets, and originally we were supposed to be their reserve force; and it was our obligation, as they said, as they told us, we would signed a six-month contract, and only after that, a three-year contract. But I didn't sign either of those contracts because I only spent four months with them until the Erdut Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Next line that needs a correction, paragraph 45, line 2 currently reads: "Platoon and unit commanders and personnel were allocated." Did you correct this to read in English: "Platoon and squad commanders and personnel were allocated"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I remember that. I simply noticed in the statement that there's reference of platoon commanders and unit commanders, because this is absurd. One could only say platoon commanders and squad commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Next correction, paragraph 47, second sentence currently reads: "It had been demolished by NATO bombing." Did you correct this sentence to read: "It had been damaged by NATO bombing"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I corrected it by saying that it had been damaged. Maybe lately destroyed, but I didn't see it. If you're referring to the police station in Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you. Next correction paragraph 54, lines 5 and 6 currently read: "The man was taken from the group by some Skorpions. I heard that the man was killed in a nearby tea house." Did you correct this passage to read: "The man was taken from the group by some policemen. I heard that the man was killed in a nearby tea house"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I corrected it because it wasn't members of the Skorpions that took the man out, but some policemen. Now, whether they were also reservists but not members of our group, whether they are policemen of the PNP. They're not Special Anti-Terrorist Units for sure, but the Skorpions did not take the man out, some policemen did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you and last correction paragraph 69, lines 4 and 5 currently read: "The platoon and unit commanders were equipped with Motorolas, radios for communication." Did you correct this passage to read: "The platoon and squad commanders were equipped with Motorola radios for communication"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same mistake that I noticed before. Instead of the word "squad," the word "unit" is used. After all, a unit is a larger formation than a squad. So most probably, this applied to squad and platoon commanders. That is why I corrected it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, other than for those corrections, are you satisfied that the information contained in this statement is accurate and true to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The information is correct according to my mind. They correspond to the truth as I saw it on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the statement at this stage and ask that it be received it's 65 ter 02224.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00493, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, did you also previously testify before this court in the trial against Milutinovic et al in July 2006?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but I did testify in the Milutinovic et al trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to go over your testimony from that case?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I listened to the audio recording in the preparatory talk with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And having had the opportunity to listen again to your previous testimony, if you were asked the same questions that you were asked during your testimony in that case would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Madam Prosecutor speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I would try to provide the same answers, but there is the problem of time and memory failures. Now you've reminding me of that testimony during the proofing, but I would do my best. I can't provide a different testimony to the one I gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the prior transcript of this witness testimony into evidence in the Milutinovic case. We have unredacted version that needs to be tendered under seal. This is 65 ter 05185 and the public redacted version is 05185.01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 05185, Your Honours, will be assigned P00494 under seal. And 65 ter number 05185.01 will be assigned P00495.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now will proceed to read the summary of this witness evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Madam Prosecutor speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. I'm having a problem with my headphones and the sound is going off, and that's why I'm pausing but I'll try to speak up. So I'm going to proceed to read the summary of this witness evidence. The witness is a former member of the Skorpions. He describes how in 1999 just before the NATO bombing commenced Slobodan Medic, also known as Boca, told him that he was needed since the old Skorpion Unit would be re-organised or reformed. The witness and around 120 men were deployed to Kosovo as members of the Skorpions. The witness describes how they were issued with equipment, hats, and uniforms which had both a SAJ patch and a Skorpion patch. The witness describes that the Skorpion Unit arrived to the village of Podujevo in Kosovo. He explains how upon arrival members of the Skorpions Unit were involved in the killing of a group of Albanian civilians. The unit was later redeployed and sent back to Serbia. The witness explains that the group was recruited again around 15th April 1999; and two or three days later, the unit and other members of units of the police were deployed back to Kosovo to the municipality of Suva Reka. The witness remained in Kosovo until early May 1999, and describes the activities he carried out during his deployment. The witness also speaks about a trial held against one of the members of the Skorpions for the killing of the Albanian civilians in the village of Podujevo. That is the summary of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I now want to turn to your statement. I want to ask you some questions about the events that you described there. In paragraph -- in paragraph 34 of your statement you indicate that in 1999, two or three days prior to the commencement of the NATO bombing, you were visited by Boca and that you were informed that the old Skorpion Unit was being reformed. First of all, who is the person that is referred to as Boca in your statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Boca is Slobodan Medic. That is his nickname is Boca. He's the former commander of the Skorpion Units which existed in the territory of Djeletovci in the former Republic of Serbian Krajina. Do you want me to describe how he came to my house, and how he engaged me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to know if -- the reasons he gave you for the reorganisation of the Skorpion Units when he met you in those days in March 1999.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He said that the KLA, which was for us a terrorist organisation, had intensified its activities, and one could feel in the air that the NATO aggression was forthcoming. I think those were the reasons he gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you say in your statement that he told you that you would be attached to the SAJ. Could you tell us what is the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I asked him who we would be acting with, whether we would be attached to the Army of Yugoslavia or to the Ministry of the Interior, and he said that we would be attached to the Ministry of the Interior as a reserve force of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit of Serbia. You asked me what SAJ was. What I have just said, SAJ is a Special Anti-Terrorist Unit of the MUP of Serbia. I would say the most elite and most highly qualified unit. Each member of this unit is highly qualified. It is the elite unit of the public security. Their active-duty members are active-duty policemen with secondary or higher police education. They have -- undergo rigorous training. And the initial training is a minimum of six months. After that the candidate works in the unit for three years and takes part in actions passively, not actively. It is only after three years that he becomes a full-fledged member of such a unit. That is why I am saying that they were the elite unit of the Ministry of the Interior. And also, they do not admit civilian persons but only members of the MUP can become their members.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was your reaction when you heard that you would be -- the Skorpions Unit would be reformed and attached to the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I personally felt pride because I considered to have considerable wartime experience, but to take part in an action side by side with some highly qualified people such as the members of the SAJ were, it was an honour even though the job we were preparing for was a dangerous one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was it regular for -- procedure for persons like yourself to be incorporated into such an elite unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I don't know. It wasn't customary for NATO to bomb us every day. This was an extraordinary situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, were you told who was going to be commanding this -- this Skorpions Unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: During his first visit, when Slobodan Medic sounded the alarm and asked us to organise, he didn't say who would be the commander. We knew that he would be our commander. But from the media, I knew that Zivko Trajkovic was the commander of this special unit, and that's all. I didn't know anything more than that regarding the structure of that unit and the commanding members.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your -- in your statement, in paragraph 37 through 39, you described how this unit was organised, and you say that on 24th March, approximately 120 volunteers and yourself were -- travelled in buses to Boca's house in Novi Sad. And in paragraph 40 you say that at Boca's house you were joined by Boca, his brother Dragan, and other volunteers. Do you recall approximately how many volunteers joined your unit in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The majority of volunteers met around the fire brigade centre in Sid, and to the best of my recollection there were three buses parked there. So we filled one bus, and some men got into the second bus. Then we moved on to Novi Sad, to the street of Sandor Peterfield, which is Mr. Medic's address, and there another 20 or 30 witnesses -- I beg your pardon. It's obviously the testimony that is putting a strain on me. Another 20 or 30 volunteers; and Milan Milanovic Mrgud; and a driver, an associate of his, were there. And from there we drove on to the town of Ruma. We were expecting some more reinforcements there, so we filled two buses, and one bus was turn back because it was empty, and these two buses headed towards Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So in total how many men approximately were in this unit by the time that you headed to Belgrade from Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but not less than 120. I'm sorry, because after all that is the capacity of two buses, about a hundred and twenty men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement that when you were heading from Novi Sad to Belgrade you also saw a man that you knew by the name of Mrgud. Could you tell us what is the full name of this person that you describe as Mrgud in your statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I've already told you. It's Milan Milanovic, known as Mrgud. I knew him from before. He was in the ministry of defence of the so-called republic of Serbian Krajina. So before the peaceful reintegration and the Erdut Agreement. After that Erdut Agreement I didn't know where he was nor where he was living. I saw them then, and he went with us as far as Prolom Banja. Before Kosovo, he would also escort us to other locations, so I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say before Kosovo he had escorted you to other locations, which locations are you referring to that he had escorted you to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, he was always -- there is an escort when we went out into the field, that is to say, when we were taking our troops out of a permanent base and we were going to a different area. To the theatre of war he accompanied us in organised transportation to Velika Kladusa before that, Bihac, and afterwards, Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know why it was that he would escort you each time you were deployed to each one of these locations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, before the Erdut Agreement, I thought it was right for him to accompany us. After all, he was a certain -- who held a certain post at the ministry of defence of the Republic of the Serb Krajina. As for the last thing in Kosovo, the Republic of the Serb Krajina no longer existed and that ministry as such. So I really don't know what his function was and how come he escorted us to Kosovo as well. I cannot say. I can just wonder a bit. He probably held some kind of post in the then-Serbia too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement at paragraph 41 that when you arrived to a field outside of Belgrade, you were issued with uniforms and weapons; and you say that your uniform had both a SAJ patch insignia and a Skorpion patch. Was this the regular type of uniform worn by members of the SAJ or was this a uniform that only your unit wore?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean I cannot say exactly, but it was somewhere near Bubanj Potok. The reason why, this was outside some kind of infrastructural premises was the NATO bombing. That is to say, boxes were taken out into some kind of a meadow or whatever and that's where we got our uniforms, complete uniforms, that is. On the caps there were insignia of the MUP of Serbia, the tricolour flag, the Serbian flag. Srdjan Manojlovic distributed Skorpion insignia to us. If he didn't have enough SAJ insignia for all of them -- well, very few people had such insignia. Probably he's the one who gave them to them. But everybody had a Serbian tricolour and Skorpion insignia. And a few had SAJ insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was this the regular uniform of the SAJ, a uniform with both a Skorpion's insignia and a SAJ patch?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't understand what regular SAJ uniform would be. The SAJ has many uniforms for different situations. This was a uniform that was along the NATO pattern. I assumed that it was our factory Mile Dragic that manufactured them. Never mind. But it is according to the NATO pattern.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That I understand. I'm just asking about the patches. Do other members of the SAJ, the regular members of the SAJ, did they usually wear uniforms with a Skorpion's patch on one arm and a SAJ patch on the other? That's what I'm asking about. Or was that specific for your unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, that's impossible. The Skorpions were something different, and the SAJ just wears its own insignia, that is to say, insignia regulated by state regulations. The Skorpions I very much doubt that the state regulated their insignia. However, I don't have any proof for or against. At any rate, SAJ members certainly do not wear Skorpion insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, when you were speaking about the distribution of insignias, you referred to a man by the name Srdjan Manojlovic. Could you tell us who that person is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Srdjan Manojlovic was a member of the Skorpions earlier on, too. He was the number two man in the Skorpions, in the preceding period, that is. He was the deputy commander, Medic's deputy; although later Medic appointed another man as deputy but regardless of that, the true function of deputy was carry out by Srdjan Manojlovic. Quite simply, he was a trained officer, commissioned or non-commissioned, of the Yugoslav Army, but at any rate he was an active-duty officer in the Yugoslav Army up until 1992 or 1993, and then he left the Yugoslav People's Army and transferred to the Skorpions. That is to say that he was a man who had all the necessary education for that kind of job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, in paragraph 44, you describe how you later travelled to Prolom Banja, to a spa there, and you indicate in paragraph 45 that there were several recruit volunteers with no combat experience and that you gave them a quick training in 24 hours. Was this the only training that was provided to these volunteers with no combat experience, this training that you provided in 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't put it that way. Fifty per cent had no combat experience whatsoever in the previous periods. I'm actually referring to the front in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. So I was surprised too. I noticed that many did not even know how to deconcer [phoen] their personal weapons. I said that to the commander and then he told me that together with a few other men I should carry out some short training, whatever, just to teach some people how to use an automatic rifle, how it is cleaned. And I tried to tell them how they should go through that terrain, Kosovo, and survive nevertheless. Yes, I also wondered, too, how come we had so many outsiders as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You had described earlier when I asked you about the SAJ you had said it was an elite unit and now you're telling me that about 50 per cent of the volunteers had no combat experience. Was it a regular procedure for such an elite unit to accept or admit such a high number of volunteers with no previous combat experience or training?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You see, specialists from the SAJ in peacetime have no need for a reserve force. That is to say that these were extraordinary circumstances. I don't know. We, the Skorpions, or the unit that was called the Skorpions, perhaps during our stay in Kosovo they could have reassigned us -- reassigned us to a reserve unit of the PJP or whatever. Now, why were we attached? Well, we were not actually members of the SAJ. We were just a reserve force. The chiefs could have probably transferred us from one unit to another, but I don't know that. I'm just assuming that. We were in the SAJ probably on someone's recommendation, and perhaps did the members of the SAJ no at all that there were so many inexperienced people there. Maybe Medic had fooled them or tried to fool them, but I'm just guessing now. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you described an incident that took place once you were deployed to Kosovo, to Podujevo, and I would like to bring up at this stage 65 ter 02229. And while that is being brought up, I -- we were speaking about the training received and you -- you explained how they -- you gave them some quick training in these 24 hours. Was any training given to these volunteers at Prolom Banja on how to treat civilians that they may encounter during their activities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I personally underwent such training. Twice, as a matter of fact. Once in 1987 in Pristina when I did my military service in the Yugoslav People's Army. The Geneva Conventions and the laws and customs of war, that is something that all soldiers are taught. The other time was on Mount Tara when I underwent this additional training at the Omorica Hotel. I personally did not give instructions to anyone, and no one issued that kind of an order that these other soldiers, these outsiders, be given this kind of training. So quite simply, no, no, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement you describe an incident that occurred --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, it's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not an objection, Your Honour. I just wanted to ask something. I was listening to the Milutinovic transcript, and I know that in relation to these names here there were some numbers, and I wanted to ask whether we are talking in terms of numbers or in terms of names. Let us agree on that in advance. We're in open session, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand the point my learned colleague is making. I was just going to get to that and ask the witness about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise the document that is up before you on your screen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: This is me trying to sketch the place where this unfortunate incident occurred in Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: On this document you've written down a number of names. When you testified before in the Milutinovic case and also attached to your statement is a redacted version of this same document without the names. Could you explain why when at the time when you testified in the Milutinovic case you had a problem with making public the names that are indicated on this document that you have prepared?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me about the time when I testified in the trial of Milan Milutinovic and others, then I insisted that the names not be mentioned in public session for a simple reason. These men were free at the time, they were at liberty, and it wasn't right for me to disclose their names in The Hague and they hadn't even been indicted. Something bad could have happened to me, to my nearest and dearest, my family. At this point in time, these persons have been prosecuted. The Serbian police and the prosecutor's office have done their job, and right now they're being tried for this crime. I don't see why we should use any kind of codes now. I think we can use their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I think that response to my learned colleague's concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now if we could zoom in a bit on this -- this sketch here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your statement, and this is at paragraph 50, you indicate that once upon arrival to Podujevo you and your colleague Milovan Tomic went off to find a suitable house for your accommodation. Have you drawn this house here on the sketch that we have before us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Could you give me a pointer or something? I did mark this. Would you like me to indicate things?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. You can indicate with the pen that is being handed to you. So if you could mark the house where you said you and your colleague found -- or intended to use as accommodation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You need to draw. The pen that you have in your hand, it's like a regular pen, so you need to draw on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: With the usher could kindly assess the witness and show him how this works.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During my very short stay in that street in Podujevo, and I'll mark the houses that I managed to enter. I'll use numbers 1, 2, 3. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is fine. So first the house that you and your colleague intended to use as accommodation. If you mark that with a 1.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: My platoon had planned to use this house, number 1, or this house, number 2. We were also thinking about which one of the two we should use.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement that you saw in a courtyard a group -- a number of the Skorpions bringing a group of Albanian civilians at gunpoint. Could you draw a circle around -- if the courtyard is visible here on the sketch, could you draw a circle around where this courtyard is located?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I can. The group of Albanian civilians escorted not only by the Skorpions and by other men, too, I wasn't paying attention, it was brought from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where would be the location of the courtyard where you saw them for the first time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: When I first saw them, I was at the entrance door of this house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say in your statement, and this is at paragraph 52, that you saw some members of the Skorpions searching these -- these civilians and that you decided to stop them from the searching. Why did you decide to stop them from searching the civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It wasn't only my decision, it was Milovan Tomic's and my own with the support of yet another man and I've forgotten his name, namely that these women should not be searched. It is embarrassing to search women. It's usually women who search women. And I saw that there were a lot of young children there. Simply I thought that it would be best to take them out into the street then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any men in this group of civilians or was it only women and children?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, there was a man, too, an older man. I cannot tell how old he was but say between the age of 50 and 70. It is really hard for me to tell. I can remember what he looked like. He had the traditional white cap that Albanians from Kosovo wear. He was the only man that I saw there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just before we move on, you have marked a series of As on your sketch. What does each A represent? What do they stand for, the As on the sketch?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I'm not much of an expert. It's not that I could do an excellent drawing. With the letter A I wanted to show that all of these were residential buildings, houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were telling us that you stopped this -- the -- the member of the Skorpion from searching the civilians, and in your statement you indicated that you decided to take the group of civilians outside to the street. Do we see this street where you took this group to here on this sketch, and if you could indicate the direction in which the civilians were taken.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The civilians were taken out of this yard in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now you've drawn a series of blue and green dots there on -- on the street. What do the blue dots stand for that you've drawn there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, the blue dots are the police. They had some kind of blue camouflage uniforms. The green dots are men in uniforms who had NATO-patterned uniforms. That could have been us, the Skorpions, members of the SAJ, and perhaps members of the PJPs, if any, but at that point in time, I only distinguished between two types of uniforms in that street. Without going into a discussion regarding the emblems on the uniforms, I'm just talking about what the uniforms looked like and what camouflage colour they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. You have also drawn an X below where your arrow ends. It's also an X, and you've drawn an arrow that indicates 35 to 40 metres. Can you explain what that depicts, that red X that you've drawn and the line of 35 to 40 metres?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The line that was drawn 30 to 40 metres, well, that's what it seemed like to me, the distance between me and the location where the X is. The X represents the place where this man, this Albanian man, this civilian, was separated from the group of women and children. Although, you asked me this a bit too early. We should have said before that that we had let the women and children go in this direction, towards the corner of the street, because we had assumed that the command was there, people who were high-ranking officers, and they probably knew how they would treat them, because we could not leave them to sleep with us. So the X is a place where the man was separated from that group and was taken into some kind of catering facility that was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you explain what happened to the group of women and children once they were out on the street, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, they walked in the direction that we had indicated to them. They -- well, I mean, from my point of view they got close to the place where the man had been, and then out of this group of policemen in the street one man said, "Why did you take that out into the street? Take that back into the yard." And then he said very loud, "Tomorrow when --" he didn't explain very much. He said, "Don't take that out into the street. Take that back into the yard." The women heard that - I assume that they knew Serbian - and they turned around themselves and walked back the same way. They went through the yard. Tomic and I and another man or two were there at the entrance into that yard, and then there's this passageway, this passageway here. It is very special. In Srem we call this an unfor [phoen] passageway, so it looks like a tunnel because it is sealed off on all sides. So the women --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] if I can just stop you there, so we can understand the sequence of events. So you said that the women and children walked in the direction where you've marked the X and the man was separated from the group. What happened to the man who was separated from the group? If you know.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The interpreter said men in the plural. There was just one man. This man was killed. He was killed with a machine-gun. I think it was an M-84. I did not see the killing, I just heard the burst of gun-fire, because he was not killed out in the street. He was killed indoors. But other members of my unit said that he was killed by some policeman from this heavy weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the women and children were sent back into -- in the direction where they came. Where were you when the women and children were sent back into the courtyard? If you can mark that with a 3 on the -- on the sketch.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I can, but I think it would be better to give me a new drawing so that it wouldn't be confusing. I didn't mark anything with a number 1 or 2 so that you would know what this is all about. Or if you want to, I can use this same sketch. It's no problem for me. So would you like me to mark this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yeah, just mark this one. If you want, you can draw a circle of where you were when the women were sent back into -- in the direction where they came from, back into the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: So the women and children returned from here in this direction. I'll mark it this way. And I was standing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just for the clarity of the transcript, the witness has drawn a broken line to indicate the direction in which the women and children returned into the courtyard and he has drawn a circle right above to the left of the number 1 that he had drawn earlier on the sketch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is an X in red toward the lower edge. What does that signify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it now. This should be lowered or taken up or down, I don't know. Are you perhaps referring to this X?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the X, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh. That's the place that I tried to explain where the man was separated from the women. The man did not go back with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, could you describe to the Court what happened when the women and children were taken back into the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No. No. They went back on their own. No one escorted them. People stood in the street, but no one was escorting them, and no one walked after them. I'll try to draw it here now. I was there with Milan Tomic and -- Tomic Milovan, and I decided that we would not spend the night in house number 2, rather, we tried to look for a house on this side of the street. We were watching this and wondering what would be good for us. The women passed by us, and they went through this corridor that looks like a tunnel, as I've already explained to you, and they went to this location here. After a minute or a minute and a half, me and Tomic and a few other soldiers were standing here. I can't remember their names. I've forgotten them. I think one of them was Nebojsa Zekic, but I'm not absolutely certain. A minute later, when those women had passed and we -- they were no longer in our scope of vision, we heard bursts of fire from several automatic rifles in an irregular manner, which means that they didn't start firing at the same time. I grant that a maximum of five automatic rifles took part in this, and I also believe that each of those automatic rifles fired a minimum of 25 shots, and I can claim this on the basis of my early experience from the battle-front, and I know how long it takes for an automatic rifle to empty all its bullets. Shall I describe the whole event to the end? As soon as I heard the shooting, my reflex was to run from this position towards this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before you continue, I'm just going to clarify the transcript so we know what the markings are. Number 3, 4, and 5 are -- are the locations that the witness indicated were the houses where they went to search with his colleague Tomic as an alternative accommodation to house number 2. The circle under number -- around red dots above house number 2 indicates the location where the civilians were in when they returned to the courtyard. I wonder, Your Honours, if we could admit this into evidence and move on to a clean copy so we can have the witness indicate the rest of the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Markings made on 65 ter 02229, Your Honours, will be P00496.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we can now have a clean copy of this same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you were telling us that you had returned -- that you heard the shooting. And can you indicate where you went once you heard the shooting? If you could draw that on -- you were doing that in the earlier sketch before I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I'll do that. At the time of the shooting, unconsciously I knew that the shooting had not come from the KLA towards us, so I ran. I never thought about anything while I was running. This is about 6 or 7 metres away. And I ran in this direction, and this is where I wanted to go. However, about here I was caught up by my friend Milovan Tomic who caught me by the arm and said, "Stand there, you fool. Don't get blood on your hands." When the shooting calmed down entirely, I managed to peep round the corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you please put a 1 where your colleague stopped you and a number 2 where you eventually stopped.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: This is where my colleague stopped me, and after the shooting, I managed to get this far. With him, not just myself. The two of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how much time went by before -- between the time that you heard the shooting and you got to the point that you've marked on the sketch as number 2? Just approximately.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It is rather hard to be precise now. A minute, maybe a few seconds longer. That is what I think. Let's say a maximum of 70 seconds. That is what I believe. Plus this brief conversation here at the position number 1 when -- when he told me, "Stop there." I think it was a maximum of 70 seconds, but in the meantime the shooting had already ceased. The shooting didn't last long either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court what you saw when you got to position number -- that you've marked number 2 on the sketch? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You see, I would say that it took a maximum of 30 seconds while I was watching the location of this tragedy, because already by then all the men, the policemen and Skorpions, tried to evacuate from that courtyard. They were leaving. I'm not saying the men who took part in the execution, but other men saw that something had happened that shouldn't have happened; and everyone tried to get away from this, some of them taking this direction, others taking this direction. So that the last that I can remember of those 20 seconds was the picture that I saw here and that I have tried to depict for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you explain what it is that you saw? You can do so by using the sketch. I see you have drawn a number 1. What does this stand for, the number 1?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Number 1 represents a member of the Skorpions. I drew this a long time ago, but I can't see the legend, but I'll try and recall the order of the men. If I make a mistake, it's only because of memory loss. I think number 1 depicts Dragan Medic. Number 2, I think, was Borojevic. Number 3 could be Demirovic. No, Demirovic was number 4; he was the last one I saw, and I couldn't see him very well. Number 6, I think, was young Zicko [phoen], but I'm not sure. Number 5 should be a policeman who couldn't have taken part in the execution because he was behind the back of these others. So I don't know exactly. Now, I can't remember exactly. I drew this several years ago when my memory was fresh, but it's always possible for me to have been mistaken. Number -- I may have mixed the order. Number 2 may have been number 3 and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in addition to seeing these members of your unit there, what else did you see was happening in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: After -- after the shooting or before the shooting? What else I saw?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you arrived there, what -- what was it that you saw? You referred to it as a tragedy that you saw for 30 minutes -- 30 seconds. What exactly did you see?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I saw - I don't know how to put it - a pile of people, and I realised immediately that they were those same women and children. I couldn't see whether anyone was alive nor whether any of the soldiers was trying to shoot them again. The term we use is "certify." I didn't see that. To make sure they were dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In paragraph 56 you say that when the shooting cease -- the shooting had just ceased and you saw a person by the name of Sasa Cvetan. Is this person also indicated here in your sketch?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I must have. You're giving me my own drawing, and I don't see the legend that I myself wrote. Yes, Sasa Cvetan is there. Now, whether he is number 1 or number 2, I can't tell. When you were proofing me two days ago for this testimony, I didn't learn this sketch by heart to be able to tell you now. Yes, Sasa Cvetan was there, Dragan Medic was there. Borojevic Dragan was there. Now, what's his name, this other guy. I'm a bit confused now. Now, what was his name? Dejan Demirovic. Yes. So there were several men there. In my mind and judging by all I know, I'm confident that the four of them carried out the execution, no others than they.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why do you say that you're confident that the four of them carried out the execution?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You see, Madam Prosecutor, after the Kumanovo Agreement, I'm confident on the basis of what I saw and what I learnt about the unit later. Our security services knew this as well, because after the Kumanovo Agreement, Sasa Cvetan was arrested and then Demirovic was arrested. I think they were arrested by the state security. They spent 10 or 20 days in detention, they were released whether it was to defend themselves at liberty. In any case, a trial was started. Cvetan Sasa was convicted, and Demirovic fled to Canada. So two men that I am confident did the shooting, their names were known by our own security services; and they were taken to court. As for the others, they were also indicted, but now there's a trial ongoing called Podujevo 2. They have charged an absolutely innocent man apart from these that I consider to be the murderers. It's not just my opinion that they killed those civilians, but the police also discovered this much later. I have to tell you that I took part twice in the trial of Sasa Cvetan. Once it was in the south of Serbia. I lied then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: And then I testified in Belgrade, and that is when I said what had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have further questions for you in relation to this incident and what you have just described. Unfortunately, we've run out of time today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could tender this exhibit, the drawing that has been marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00497, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We -- as the Prosecutor has indicated, we have reached the time where we need to adjourn for the evening. We continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. The court officer will show you out after we leave and will give you assistance about your presence here tomorrow morning. We must ask that you return tomorrow to complete your evidence. Over the break overnight, you should not speak to any person about the evidence that you are giving. We adjourn to resume at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of March, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.
